content_html:
A defined-benefit pension pays a set monthly income for life, but retiring with one usually means making a few one-time choices that can't be undone. This calculator helps with the three most common: taking a lump sum instead of monthly payments, choosing a single-life or joint-and-survivor payout, and deciding whether a bigger pension is worth working a few more years for.

How to use this calculator

  1. Decision to compare: pick one of the three choices. The form shows only the fields that decision needs.
  2. Pension amounts: take these from your plan's benefit statement or election package. Use gross monthly amounts.
  3. Your life expectancy: payments are counted up to this age. Being cautious and using an age a few years beyond your average expectancy is common.
  4. Investment return: the yearly return you could realistically earn if you managed the money yourself. It is used to put payments made at different times on an equal footing.
  5. Yearly pension increase: the cost-of-living adjustment (COLA), if your plan has one. Many private pensions have none.

How the values are worked out

Every option is turned into a single figure: its value at the age payments start. Each monthly payment is discounted back at your investment return, so a dollar paid at 80 counts for less than a dollar paid at 65. The option with the higher value is the better deal on these assumptions.

For the lump sum decision, the calculator also finds the investment return at which the pension and the lump sum are worth exactly the same. That is the return you would need to beat to come out ahead by taking the cash, and it is often the most useful number on the page. It also shows how long the lump sum would last if you paid yourself the same monthly income.

For the work-longer decision, both pensions are valued at the earlier retirement age, and the break-even age shows when the larger, later pension would have paid out the same total in dollars.

Worked examples

Lump sum or monthly pension

At 65 you are offered $500,000 or $3,000 a month rising 2% a year. With a life expectancy of 85 and a 5% investment return, the pension is worth about $542,147, $42,147 more than the lump sum. You would need to earn about 6.0% a year on the lump sum to match it, and drawing $3,000 a month (plus increases) from the lump sum would empty it at about 82 and 11 months.

Single life or joint and survivor

The same retiree can take $3,000 a month for their own life or $2,700 a month with 50% continuing to a spouse who is 62 now and expected to live to 88. The single-life pension is worth $542,147 and the joint option $537,508, so on these numbers single life is ahead by $4,638. The joint option pays more in total, $939,086 against $874,705, because the spouse collects $1,350 a month for about six more years.

Retire now or work longer

Retiring at 62 pays $2,400 a month; waiting until 65 pays $3,000. At a 5% return and 2% increases, the earlier pension is worth $479,700 at age 62 and the later one $468,327. The later pension catches up in total dollars at about age 79 and 3 months. At a 3% return the result flips in favor of waiting.

Points to weigh beyond the numbers

  • A pension pays for as long as you live, so it protects against outliving your savings. A lump sum doesn't.
  • A lump sum can be left to heirs and gives you flexibility for large expenses.
  • Private pensions are insured by the Pension Benefit Guaranty Corporation up to legal limits; a lump sum depends on how you invest it.
  • Rolling a lump sum directly into an IRA avoids immediate tax. Taking it as cash makes it taxable income in that year.
  • Choosing single life usually requires your spouse's written consent.

faq.question: Is it better to take a pension lump sum or monthly payments?
faq.answer: It depends on how long you expect to live, what return you could earn on the money, whether the pension rises with inflation and how much you value guaranteed income. Compare the implied return of the pension with a return you could realistically earn; if you can't comfortably beat it, the monthly pension is usually the better value.

faq.question: How do interest rates affect a pension lump sum?
faq.answer: Plans convert monthly benefits into lump sums using interest rates set by IRS rules. When those rates are higher, the lump sum offered for the same monthly pension is smaller, and when they fall, lump sums grow.

faq.question: What does a 50% joint-and-survivor pension mean?
faq.answer: You receive a reduced monthly pension for your lifetime, and if you die first, your spouse keeps receiving half of that amount for the rest of their life. A 100% option keeps the full amount going but starts lower.

faq.question: Are pension payments taxable?
faq.answer: Pension payments are generally taxed as ordinary income at the federal level, except any part that comes from after-tax contributions you made. Some states exempt all or part of pension income.

faq.question: Does this calculator include taxes?
faq.answer: No. It compares gross amounts. Both monthly payments and lump-sum withdrawals are usually taxable, so taxes tend to affect the options similarly, as long as a lump sum is rolled over rather than cashed out.
